n: In this lecture we will consider the topic of metal compounds and mineralisation. The outline is as follows: absorption of metal compounds in the body, methods of mineralisation, preparing the mineralisate for analysis, and masking interfering ions. We study the group of poisonous metal compounds that are isolated from a biological object by mineralisation and must be analysed in forensic chemical practice. Key terms: metal compounds, mineralisation, denitration, the fractional method and masking.

t: Group of Metallic Poisons and Absorption
n: First let us consider the group of metallic poisons. Heavy metals, arsenic As and antimony Sb are present in the poisonous and potent substances of this group. Absorption and elimination of metal-containing poisons take place in the respiratory tract, that is, in the alveoli. They also take place in the mucous membranes of the gastrointestinal tract, in blood vessels and in various membranes. In the gastrointestinal tract, metal compounds are absorbed into the blood mainly in the small intestine.

t: Transformations of Compounds That Have Entered the Body
n: Compounds that have entered the body change along the way. PbCO3 or BaCO3 entering the stomach is converted into chlorides under the action of the acid of gastric juice. In the alkaline medium of the intestinal and pancreatic juices they are converted back into carbonates. In the large intestine, metals form sulphides. Absorption in the body depends on the form of the compound: organometallic compounds are absorbed better than inorganic ones.

Now change of valency and toxicity. Metal compounds with variable valency are oxidised and reduced in the body. For example, As(+5) passes into the As(+3) state, that is, a state with a stronger toxic action, and forms stable complexes with proteins. Mercury in the metallic state is oxidised to a higher valency, to Hg2+, and has a strong toxic action.

Metals form complexes with proteins. Mercury, lead, copper, zinc, cadmium, nickel and cobalt form stable coordination compounds with proteins, that is, albuminates. The complexes are formed with the functional groups of proteins, peptides and amino acids, such as –COOH, –SH, –NH2. Histidine and cysteine are given as examples. Nucleic and citric acids, and the –OH, –PO3H and –SO3H groups, are also important in complex formation.

Why is mineralisation needed? Metal compounds are distributed in the blood and tissue fluids in the form of ions and neutral molecules. Free ions quickly leave the blood. Large complex and colloidal compounds are retained in the liver and spleen, and dispersed colloids circulate in the blood vessels for a long time. To isolate them, it is necessary to convert them to the ionic state. For this purpose, the object is mineralised, that is, burnt and converted to the ionic state.

t: The 13 Metals to Be Tested For
n: According to the orders on forensic medical examination, it is necessary to test for 13 metals. They are divided by analytical groups. In group 2 there is Ba, in group 3 Mn, Cr, Zn, Tl, in group 4 Pb, Cu, Hg, Cd, Ag, Bi. Group 5 has As and Sb, which are tested in the trivalent and pentavalent states.

Mineralisation methods are divided into two groups: dry ashing and the wet method. Dry ashing methods are particular methods used to isolate non-volatile metal cations. The wet method is mineralisation in an acidic medium in the presence of various oxidising agents. It is a general method, applicable to all metals except mercury.

Dry ashing methods. The first is simple ashing. The second is ashing with added oxidising agents: H2O2, NH4NO3, HNO3, HNO3 with H2O2, and also NaNO3 with Na2CO3. The ash-like residue formed in ashing is dissolved in a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, filtered, and the filtrate evaporated to dryness. After the residue is dissolved in water, it is tested for non-volatile cations.

t: History of Mineralisation: Nelyubin and the Chlorine Method
n: Let us briefly dwell on the history of mineralisation. The need for mineralisation in order to determine metallic poisons was theoretically substantiated in 1824 by the Russian scientist Nelyubin. In 1844 the French chemists Fresenius and Babo proposed a method of treating the object with liberated chlorine. This method was used in forensic chemistry for more than 100 years. It arose on the basis of the method of decolourisation with gaseous chlorine proposed in 1820 by Dufeau and Millon. Later, in 1902 Meyler and in 1908 Ravnadix considered the H2SO4 and HNO3 method, and in 1932 Cahn the H2SO4, HNO3 and HClO4 method.

The reaction of the chlorine method: KClO3 + 6HCl = 3Cl2 + KCl + 3H2O. Then Cl2 + HOH → HCl + HClO, and next HClO → HCl + O. Treatment with chlorine is convenient mainly for determining mercury. There are also disadvantages: organic substances are destroyed incompletely, and it takes 18-20 hours to burn 100 g of object. In the analysis of arsenic and mercury there are many losses, and the large final volume reduces sensitivity. Adding an excess of oxidising agent is dangerous: an explosion may occur.

t: Mineralisation with Sulphuric and Nitric Acids
n: Mineralisation with sulphuric and nitric acids. In 1908 the Russian scientist Ravnadix, and in 1902 Meyler, studied mineralisation with sulphuric and nitric acid in depth. It was recommended that the acids be in a ratio of 1:4 to the object. The method is based on oxidation of the object by atomic oxygen liberated as a result of the reactions.

t: Atomic Oxygen and Convenience of the Method
n: Atomic oxygen is formed in several reactions: H2SO4 → H2SO3 + O, HNO3 → HNO2 + O, H2O2 → H2O + O and 2HNO2 → N2 + H2O + 3O. The conveniences of this method: organic compounds are completely destroyed, it takes relatively little time, and a small volume of mineralisate is obtained. The disadvantage is that almost all the mercury is lost. A Kjeldahl flask and a separatory funnel are used as the apparatus.

The method of Stepanov and Neumark is based on mineralisation in the presence of sulphuric acid and ammonium nitrate. The reaction: H2SO4 + 2NH4NO3 → 2HNO3 + (NH4)2SO4. In this method the object is not only oxidised but also nitrated. A large amount of the salt (NH4)2SO4 forms in the mineralisate. Mineralisation proceeds more completely than in the chlorine method, but not to the end.

Now mineralisation with H2SO4 and H2O2, that is, perhydrol. This method has had almost no practical significance. The reasons: complete mineralisation does not occur, and expensive perhydrol must be used. The convenience of the method is that at the end of the reaction no excess of nitrogen oxidising agents remains.

The Cahn method. In 1932 the French scientist Cahn proposed mineralisation in the presence of sulphuric, nitric and perchloric acids. In this method mineralisation proceeds completely, and the metals are in the higher valency state. But remember: perchloric acid is extremely dangerous and can form highly flammable and explosive products.

Let us compare the wet mineralisation methods. In the chlorine method, organic substances are destroyed incompletely and 18-20 hours are needed for 100 g of object, but it is convenient for determining mercury. In the H2SO4 and HNO3 method, destruction is complete, the method is rapid, and the volume of mineralisate is small, but mercury is almost lost. H2SO4 and NH4NO3 is more complete than chlorine, but not to the end. H2SO4 and H2O2 has no practical significance. The Cahn method proceeds completely, with metals in the higher valency state, but perchloric acid can form explosive products.

Preparing the mineralisate for analysis. The mineralisate obtained by the wet method is first purified from oxidising agents. This is because oxidising agents interfere with the analysis of elements such as arsenic and lead, and with the precipitation of metal cations as sulphides. The removal of oxidising agents depends on the method by which mineralisation was carried out. In the chlorine method dechlorination is used, and in the presence of nitric acid, denitration.

Dechlorination proceeds as follows. The mineralisate is evaporated on a water bath at 50 °C with 5-6 times its volume of water, until the HCl concentration is about 2 percent. Excess chlorine is tested with iodine-starch paper, or pure air is passed through the mineralisate. The first method takes 12-13 hours, the second 2-3 hours. Denitration is used when mineralisation has been carried out in the presence of nitric acid or its salts.

About nitrosyl sulphuric acid. In the presence of nitric acid, HNO3, HNO2, nitrogen oxides and nitrosyl sulphuric acid are formed as oxidising agents. Of these, nitrosyl sulphuric acid is the hardest to remove. In the pure state it is a colourless crystalline substance, melts at 70 °C, and hydrolyses rapidly in moist air and in water. It usually forms if the concentration of sulphuric acid is above 57.5 percent. It dissolves in concentrated sulphuric acid, so the mineralisate is diluted.

Denitration by the hydrolysis method. The mineralisate is diluted with 5-10 parts of distilled water and evaporated until white sulphur trioxide appears. The method takes 9-17 hours. The presence of oxidising agents is checked with a solution of diphenylamine in concentrated sulphuric acid. If an oxidising agent is present, a blue colour forms.

The chemical methods of denitration are based on converting oxidising agents into volatile gases and removing them from the mineralisate. For this, formaldehyde, sulphite salts, urea or ammonium salts are used; their reactions are given in the table. Denitration takes 5-10 minutes, that is, the method is quick and easy to perform. The purified mineralisate is diluted to 180 ml and boiled, then used in determining the cations.

t: Masking by the Fractional Method: Principle
n: Now the principle of masking by the fractional method. The analysis of metals proceeds in two stages: first, the interfering ions are removed with a suitable reagent or mixture. Then the metals are identified with a reagent that gives a colour or a precipitate. Masking is based on converting the interfering ions into a stable complex, changing their valency, and changing the pH of the medium. In masking, complexone III, that is, Trilon B, and citric, tartaric and ascorbic acids are widely used.

An example of masking: cobalt and iron (III). In identifying the Co2+ ion by adding ammonium thiocyanate to form blue (NH4)2Co(CNS)4, Fe3+ interferes. This is because in the reaction Fe3+ + 3NH4CNS → Fe(CNS)3 + 3NH4+ a blood-red colour appears. To mask Fe3+, fluorides and phosphates are used. That is, Fe3+ with fluoride passes into the colourless complex [FeF6]3−.

The list of masking reagents. The reagents: cyanides, fluorides, phosphates, thiosulphates, thiourea and hydroxylamine. Glycerol and complexones are also used, that is, Trilon B, and citric, tartaric, oxalic and ascorbic acids. Citric acid masks Bi, Cu, Fe, Sb, Hg, Ag, Cd. Tartaric acid is used for masking Cu, Fe, Al, Bi, Cd, Hg, Pb, Zn.

Demasking is the release of a masked ion from the masking reagent. Example: the hexacyanoferrate(II) complex reacts with the mercury(II) ion, binding the cyanide as Hg(CN)2. As a result, the masked ion is released. The use of cyanides is explained by the fact that they can easily be released from their complexes.

Masking with cyanides. Cyanides form various complexes with the ions Cu2+, Co2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Ni2+, Zn2+, Cd2+, Hg2+ and Ag+. Copper(II) is first reduced: 2Cu(CN)2 → 2CuCN + (CN)2. Then the complex forms: CuCN + 3KCN → K3[Cu(CN)4]. Remember: cyanides are poisonous. They must not be added to acidic solutions, because in acid volatile and poisonous hydrogen cyanide forms. Experiments are carried out in a fume cupboard.

Masking with fluoride, phosphate, thiosulphate and hydroxylamine. Fluorides mask Fe3+ ions as the colourless stable complex [FeF6]3−. Phosphates under acidic conditions mask Fe3+ as [Fe(PO4)2]3−. Thiosulphates mask the ions Ag, Pb, Cu, Fe, with copper first reduced to Cu+. Hydroxylamine forms the complex [Co(NH2OH)6]2+ with Co, reduces Fe3+, and oxidises AsO2− and SbO2−. Its excess is eliminated with formaldehyde.

Masking copper with thiosulphate proceeds in two stages. First Cu2+ is reduced to Cu+, then a complex forms. First stage: CuSO4 + Na2S2O3 → CuS2O3 + Na2SO4. Second stage, reduction: 4CuS2O3 → 2Cu2S2O3 + S4O6. Third stage: Cu2S2O3 + Na2S2O3 → Na2[Cu2(S2O3)2]. This is the masking complex.

Hydroxylamine plays a dual role. With one ion it forms a complex, with another it enters an oxidation-reduction reaction. With cobalt ions the complex [Co(NH2OH)6]2+ forms. It reduces Fe3+, and oxidises the ions AsO2− and SbO2−. Excess hydroxylamine is eliminated with formaldehyde, and formaldoxime is formed.

Thiourea, glycerol and complexones. Thiourea masks the ions of bismuth, iron, antimony, cadmium, mercury, silver and others, and forms stable inner complexes. Glycerol forms glycerates with bismuth, lead and cadmium, and with some ions, for example Cu2+, gives a coloured compound. Complexone III, that is, Trilon B, masks the ions of cadmium, cobalt, copper, iron, manganese, lead, zinc and magnesium. Regardless of valency, it reacts in a 1:1 ratio.

Masking with organic acids. Citric acid and citrates mask the ions of bismuth, copper, iron(III), antimony(III), cadmium, mercury, silver and others. Oxalic acid and oxalates form water-soluble stable complexes with the ions of copper, iron, aluminium, bismuth, cadmium, mercury, lead and zinc. The masking property of ascorbic acid is based on its reducing properties. It is used for masking Fe3+ and Sn4+ ions.

Let us summarise the masking reagents according to the ions for which they are used. Citric acid masks Bi, Cu, Fe, Sb, Hg, Ag, Cd. Tartaric acid masks Cu, Fe, Al, Bi, Cd, Hg, Pb, Zn. Thiosulphates mask Ag, Pb, Cu, Fe, thiourea masks Bi, Fe, Sb, Cd, Hg, Ag, Pb, and glycerol masks Bi, Pb, Cd. Complexone III, that is, Trilon B, masks the ions Cd, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Pb, Zn, Mg and reacts with the ions in a 1:1 ratio.

Conveniences and disadvantages of the wet method. Conveniences: organic compounds are completely destroyed, it takes relatively little time, and a small volume of mineralisate is obtained. The disadvantage is that almost all the mercury is lost. A Kjeldahl flask and a separatory funnel are used for mineralisation. They are among the necessary instruments and equipment in the laboratory class.

t: Determining Metals: The H2S Method and the Fractional Method
n: Let us compare the methods of determining metals. The hydrogen sulphide method is based on separating cations by analytical groups using group precipitants. It was used until the 1970s and is not used now. Now in forensic chemical laboratories the particular fractional method, proposed by Doctor of Chemical Sciences A.N. Krylova, is widely used. The fractional method is based on isolating cations from the mineralisate by extraction and re-extraction and identifying them with specific and sensitive reactions. To eliminate the influence of other cations, complex formation, oxidation-reduction, change of pH, obtaining a small volume of mineralisate, and dilution are used.

t: Median Lethal Dose of Metallic Poisons
n: The median lethal dose of metallic poisons. For arsenic and antimony compounds LD50 = 0.08-0.1 g, for thallium 0.5 g, for chromium 0.2-1 g. For cadmium 0.03 g, for mercury 0.2-0.3 g, for ZnCl2 5.0, for KMnO4 15-20 g. For chromium and manganese, the higher-valency compounds have the stronger action, and organic compounds of mercury are strongly poisonous. Poisoning with arsenic and mercury ends in death in 50 percent of cases.

t: Signs of Poisoning and Objects of Examination
n: Signs of poisoning and objects of examination. In poisoning with heavy metal salts and arsenic, thirst, vomiting, diarrhoea, pain in the stomach and bleeding from the internal organs are observed. The colour of the vomit is green with chromium and copper compounds and brown with manganese, and a metallic taste is felt in the mouth. With lead, black spots appear on the gums, and with bismuth and mercury, white ones. Copper and zinc compounds raise body temperature to 40 °C and above. As objects, the stomach, small and large intestine, liver and gallbladder, kidney, urine, spleen, vomit, hair, nails and bones are taken.

In conclusion. Metal compounds form stable complexes with proteins in the body, so the object is mineralised for analysis. Wet mineralisation, that is, H2SO4 with HNO3, H2O2 and HClO4, is used for all metals except mercury. The mineralisate is purified from oxidising agents, that is, dechlorination and denitration are carried out. In the fractional method, interfering ions are masked: with cyanide, fluoride, phosphate, thiosulphate, Trilon B and others. This method was proposed by Krylova.
